title: SoFoNO: Arbitrary-scale image super-resolution via Sobolev Fourier neural operator

• We propose SoFoNO, a novel SISR
framework with a Sobolev branch oper-
ating in the frequency domain.
• We introduce a learnable Sobolev ex-
ponent that directly guides the Sobolev 
loss, enabling precise and visually coher-
ent reconstructions.
• We validate SoFoNO through extensive
in-scale and out-of-scale experiments, 
showing robust arbitrary-scale perfor-
mance.

G R A P H I C A L 
A B S T R A C T

Accurately reconstructing fine textures and sharp edges remains a significant challenge in Single Image Super-
Resolution (SISR) tasks, often resulting in overly smooth and less realistic images. To alleviate this issue we 
propose a novel SISR framework named Sobolev Fourier Neural Operator (SoFoNO). Central to our approach 
is a specialized architecture featuring a Sobolev Branch, which effectively captures detailed structures in the 
frequency domain via a learnable Sobolev exponent. Importantly, the learned Sobolev exponent is directly em-
ployed as derivative order parameters within the Sobolev loss function, enabling more precise and visually 
coherent reconstructions. Unlike conventional pixel-level loss functions, the Sobolev loss explicitly incorpo-
rates frequency-domain penalties, significantly enhancing the reconstruction quality of detailed image structures. 
Extensive experiments conducted on multiple datasets under both in-scale and out-scale scenarios demonstrate 
that our SoFoNO provides robust and effective performance in arbitrary-scale super-resolution, consistently 
outperforming representative existing methods across various tested scale factors without relying on attention 
mechanisms.

Single Image Super-Resolution (SISR) is a powerful technique that 
enhances the resolution of low-resolution (LR) images by reconstruct-
ing high-resolution (HR) details, resulting in clearer and more visually 
detailed representations. This technology has garnered significant at-
tention due to its wide range of applications across various domains. 
In image and video enhancement, this technology is used to restore 
and upscale old or low-resolution footage, significantly improving visual 
quality [1]. In medical imaging, SISR plays a crucial role in enhanc-
ing the clarity of diagnostic images, thereby facilitating more accurate 
analysis and early disease detection [2]. Similarly, in satellite image 
analysis, SISR enhances spatial resolution, thereby providing more pre-
cise geographical and environmental data for applications such as urban 
planning, disaster management, and land-use monitoring [3]. In addi-
tion to these fields, SR is also used as a tool to enhance the performance 
of specific tasks such as Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and object 
detection [4,5].

The development of deep neural network (DNN)-based SISR mod-
els has significantly improved image quality by continuously advancing 
network architectures and optimization techniques. Early CNN-based 
methods such as SRCNN [6] and ESPCN [7] demonstrated the feasibil-
ity of end-to-end SR, while deeper architectures like VDSR [8] and EDSR 
[9] further enhanced performance through residual learning and archi-
tectural refinements. Subsequent works including RDN [10] and RCAN
[11] introduced dense connections and attention mechanisms, achiev-
ing more effective feature representation and improved recovery of fine 
details.

However, these Fixed-Scale Super-resolution (FSSR) methods often 
focus solely on fixed integer scale factors such as x2, x4, and x8, leading 
to inefficiencies since each scale must be learned separately. To ad-
dress this limitation, Arbitrary-Scale Super-Resolution (ASSR) [12,13] 
has been proposed to reconstruct high-resolution images at any de-
sired scale, making it more suitable for real-world scenarios where 
scale requirements vary dynamically. Unlike FSSR, ASSR requires mod-
els to generalize across a continuous range of scales, which introduces 
additional challenges in capturing smoothness and fine textures.

Recent ASSR approaches have explored diverse solutions. MetaSR
[12] employs meta-learning to generate scale-specific filters, while 
Local Implicit Image Function (LIIF) [14] and Local Texture Estimator 
(LTE) [15] leverage implicit functions and frequency-domain cues to re-
construct details at arbitrary scales. More recent efforts extend this line 
of work to specialized domains [16] or probabilistic modeling [17], re-
flecting the continuous evolution of architectures toward flexible and 
high-fidelity super-resolution.

Recently, attention mechanisms [18] have been widely introduced 
in ASSR, as in many other vision tasks [19–37], to enhance feature

aggregation and improve reconstruction quality. For example, the Super-
Resolution Neural Operator (SRNO) [28] leverages Galerkin-type atten-
tion [38] to efficiently integrate kernel operations, while other methods 
[39–41] have further extended attention-based strategies for arbitrary-
scale SR. In parallel, frequency-domain approaches have also emerged, 
recognizing that high-frequency information is crucial for recovering 
fine details. FourierSR [42] leverages the Fourier transform through 
a token-based plugin to enhance high-frequency restoration, while 
lightweight adaptive feature de-drifting [43] employs discrete cosine 
transform (DCT) to stabilize compressed representations by correcting 
frequency-domain shifts. Motivated by these advances, we propose a 
Sobolev Fourier Neural Operator (SoFoNO) architecture that achieves 
robust performance without relying on attention mechanisms. By elim-
inating the computationally expensive attention operations, SoFoNO 
significantly reduces both computational cost and memory usage while 
maintaining competitive performance.

On the one hand, Sobolev training [45] has proven effective 
in various domains, including Physics-Informed Neural Networks 
(PINNs, [46]) [47] and Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) [48], 
demonstrating notable improvements in learning complex functions 
[49]. Inspired by these successes, we propose a Sobolev loss function 
for super-resolution tasks that leverages a learnable Sobolev exponent 
(s ∈ R) as the derivative order, enabling adaptive control over the 
smoothness and detail sensitivity of the learning process. In our frame-
work, the Sobolev exponent is not treated as a fixed hyperparameter 
but is instead trained within the SoFoNO architecture itself, specifi-
cally through the frequency-domain transformation. This integration 
allows the loss function to dynamically align with the characteris-
tics learned by the network. Fig. 1(a) presents quantitative results 
on the DIV2K validation set [50], showing that integrating the pro-
posed Sobolev loss leads to consistent improvements across various 
scale factors when compared with representative existing methods. 
Furthermore, as shown in Fig. 1(b), qualitative comparisons on the 
Urban100 dataset [51] confirm that our approach enables more faithful 
restoration of complex textures such as building facades and repetitive 
patterns.

• We propose a novel arbitrary-scale SISR framework, called SoFoNO,
which consists of a local branch that extracts information from the 
nearby spatial region, a Sobolev branch that captures information 
in the frequency domain via a learnable Sobolev exponent s, and a 
fusion region that effectively integrates both branches.
• We utilize the Sobolev exponent s obtained from SoFoNO as deriva-
tive order parameters within the Sobolev loss function to achieve 
more precise results.

The development of deep neural network (DNN)-based SISR mod-
els [52] has led to significant improvements in image quality. The 
SRCNN [6] was the first deep learning-based SR model, introduc-
ing a CNN architecture for the direct mapping of low-resolution to 
high-resolution images.

Since SRCNN [6], numerous DNN-based SR models have been devel-
oped. For example, ESPCN [7] improves efficiency by introducing pixel 
shuffling, which significantly reduces computational complexity and en-
ables real-time performance by shifting the upsampling process to the 
final stage. Other examples include VDSR [8] and EDSR [9], which pro-
pose methods to improve performance through residual learning, while 
EnhanceNet [53] introduces perceptual and adversarial losses to gen-
erate sharper details and more realistic textures, prioritizing visually 
pleasing reconstructions over strict pixel-wise fidelity. Moreover, RDN 
[10] improves image detail recovery by incorporating dense connections 
and hierarchical feature fusion, while RCAN [11] utilizes channel atten-
tion modules to dynamically enhance channel-specific features, thereby 
improving super-resolution performance.

On the other hand, instances of SR being integrated into and utilized 
in other fields are also emerging. For example, the Super-Resolution 
Generative Adversarial Network (SRGAN) [54], which was the first to 
introduce Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)-based [55] SR, em-
ploys adversarial learning to generate high-resolution images with more 
realistic textures and greater detail. Furthermore, Enhanced Perceptual 
Super-Resolution (EPSR) [56] explores the perception-distortion trade-
off in super-resolution by introducing an Enhanced Perceptual Super-
Resolution Network that leverages GAN-based training alongside per-
ceptual and style losses to balance natural texture representation with 
low distortion. More recently, diffusion-based SR approaches have 
emerged as a new generative paradigm. SR3 [57] adapts denoising dif-
fusion probabilistic models to image-to-image translation and performs 
super-resolution through a stochastic iterative denoising process, pro-
gressively refining Gaussian noise into photo-realistic high-resolution 
images conditioned on low-resolution inputs. StableSR [58] introduces 
a time-aware encoder and a controllable feature wrapping module 
for blind super-resolution, enabling high-quality and fidelity-balanced 
restoration without retraining the diffusion backbone.

More recent works have continued to advance both efficiency and 
representational power in SISR. The Feature Distillation Interaction 
Weighting Network (FDIWN) [59] introduces specially designed feature 
distillation and interaction weighting units to achieve a lightweight ar-
chitecture that balances accuracy and efficiency. SwinIR [24] establishes 
a strong baseline for image restoration by employing Swin Transformer 
blocks with residual connections, demonstrating that Transformer-based 
designs can effectively capture both local and global dependencies. The 
Cross-receptive Focused Inference Network (CFIN) [60] combines CNN-
based cross-scale information aggregation with Transformer modules, 
enabling more efficient receptive field utilization, while the Efficient 
Long-range Attention Network (ELAN) [25] enhances performance by 
modeling long-range dependencies with reduced computational over-
head. More recently, hierarchical and hybrid architectures such as 
Hierarchical Transformers (HiT-SR) [34], which leverage hierarchical 
windows for efficient multi-scale attention, and Feature Interaction 
Weighted Hybrid Network (FIWHN) [61], which integrates CNN and 
Transformer modules with feature interaction weighting, have im-
proved both scalability and detail recovery. The Wavelet-based Feature 
Enhancement Network (WFEN) [62] further advances this line by in-
troducing wavelet-domain feature processing tailored for facial SR. 
Finally, MambaIR [63] adapts the state-space Mamba model for image

restoration, incorporating local enhancement and channel attention, and 
demonstrates competitive results against Transformer-based baselines 
while maintaining linear complexity, highlighting a new direction for 
sequence modeling in SISR.

In general, SISR is a technology that restores low-resolution images 
to high-resolution at a specific scale factor (e.g., x2, x4, x8), requir-
ing the model to learn based on that scale factor. However, a new 
approach called ASSR, introduced by MetaSR [12], enables more flexi-
ble learning without being dependent on a specific scale factor. Thus, 
the field of SISR has been steadily evolving with the arbitrary-scale 
methodology at its core [64–68], aiming to meet a wider range of 
magnification requirements rather than relying on a fixed scale as be-
fore. Among these developments, LIIF [14], which introduced a Local 
Ensemble method based on implicit neural representations, has demon-
strated strong performance by modeling continuous coordinate-to-pixel 
mappings. LTE [15] further enhances detail reconstruction by intro-
ducing a dominant-frequency estimator that leverages Fourier-domain 
cues to better capture high-frequency components. SRNO [28] leverages 
Galerkin-type attention [38] to efficiently integrate kernel operations, 
and subsequent works [39–41] have further advanced attention-based 
strategies for arbitrary-scale SR. In sharp contrast to this prevailing 
trend, we take a fundamentally different direction by operating in 
the frequency domain, entirely avoiding attention while still deliver-
ing superior efficiency and competitive performance. This distinction 
highlights that strong arbitrary-scale SR does not necessarily require the 
computational and architectural overhead of attention based methods.

Following these advances, S3Mamba [69] introduced a scalable 
state-space model with linear complexity and scale-aware attention, 
offering a new operator design for arbitrary-scale SR. Subsequently, 
ContinuousSR [70] proposed a Pixel-to-Gaussian paradigm that recon-
structs continuous HR signals via Gaussian splatting, enabling ultra-fast 
rendering across arbitrary scales. GaussianSR [44] represented each 
pixel as a continuous Gaussian field and jointly learned encoder, clas-
sifier, and Gaussian kernels to achieve high-fidelity and interpretable 
reconstructions. Our SoFoNO is fundamentally designed within this 
evolving ASSR framework and shows consistently strong performance 
compared to representative methods, including LIIF [14], LTE [15], 
SRNO [28], and GaussianSR [44], by extracting information from the 
Fourier space via a SoFoNo block.

Sobolev training is particularly distinct from other methods in that 
it modifies the loss function to incorporate the derivative information 
[45]. This method is based on the mathematical notion of Sobolev spaces 
[71], for example W k,p , which consist of functions whose derivatives up 
to order k are in L p . For instance, in the H 1 (= W 1,2 ) space, a function and 
its first derivative must be square-integrable, ensuring a certain degree of 
smoothness. Similarly, in the H 2 (= W 2,2 ) space, this condition extends 
to the second derivative, allowing for even greater regularity.

Using these methods, neural networks can better capture the smooth-
ness and complex structure of functions [72]. This is particularly useful 
when solving partial differential equations (PDEs) [47], where accu-
rate derivative information is crucial. In this context, Sobolev Training 
has been successfully applied to Physics-Informed Neural Networks 
(PINNs) [47], allowing the network to incorporate additional derivative 
constraints and improve the accuracy of PDE solutions.

However, in vision tasks, approximation methods are commonly used 
to obtain derivatives since the derivative information is not known in 
advance. For instance, Yuan et al. [49] approximate the H 1 loss us-
ing the Finite Difference Method (FDM) [73] and apply it to INR [48], 
demonstrating improved performance. Meanwhile, research on Sobolev 
training is actively being conducted to explore various derivative ap-
proximation techniques, such as Chebyshev Spectral Methods [74]. In

this paper, we propose a Sobolev loss function that utilizes Fourier 
transformation and frequency domain variables [75].

Recently, in the field of deep learning, there has been active research 
on enhancing the expressive power of neural networks by leveraging 
numerical analysis techniques. For example, in [49], the performance 
of INR has been improved by approximating derivatives using the FDM 
[73]. This enables the neural network to be utilized in various ways, al-
lowing it to learn more sophisticated derivative information and thereby 
enhancing its capability in solving PDEs and other complex mathemat-
ical problems [76,77]. However, most approximations, including the 
finite difference method (FDM), have limitations in that they are only 
applicable when s ∈ N, such as in H 1 training or H 2 training [45,71].

To overcome this limitation, we utilize a practical approximation

In this paper, we refer to s ∈ R as the Sobolev exponent, which is 
unrestricted by integer constraints, representing the derivative order, 
and directly influencing the frequency emphasis in Eq. (1). Specifically, 
when s > 0, high-frequency components are amplified, improving fine 
details in the transformed signal. In contrast, when s < 0, the low fre-
quency components become more dominant, resulting in a smoothing 
effect. This shift in frequency emphasis varies depending on the sign of 
s, as shown in Fig. 2, which displays the transformation visual results 
for both positive and negative values of s. The results of the transforma-
tion depend on s. Compared to the original image, the version produced

with s < 0 appears to be blurrier, indicating an emphasis on lower-
frequency components. In contrast, using s > 0 restores a sharper image, 
suggesting that higher frequency components are strengthened. In this 
paper, we apply this transformation method in the Sobolev Branch 
(Section 3.2.2) of SoFoNO to effectively adjust the frequency of the 
feature map, enhancing ASSR performance from both quantitative and 
qualitative perspectives. Moreover, Eq. (1) is instantiated as a dedicated 
Sobolev block in our architecture, where the Sobolev exponent s directly 
modulates the frequency weighting. This block-wise formulation is novel 
in that it unifies the analytical expression with a learnable network 
component, thereby providing a principled mechanism for adaptive 
frequency control across scales.

x and y. Afterward, the feature map passes through T SoFoNO blocks 
(Section 3.2.2, Fig. 4), indexed by i = 0, 1, ... , T - 1. Each SoFoNO block 
refines the feature representation to capture both local and frequency

In this experiment, we utilize the DIV2K training dataset [50]. The
DIV2K dataset is a high-quality image dataset commonly used for super-
resolution tasks, containing 800 training images, 100 validation images, 
and 100 test images. The dataset consists of high-resolution (2 K) images 
that are designed to enhance the performance of image restoration and 
super-resolution models.

J.K. Oh, H. Son, H.J. Hwang et al.

For training, we repeatedly apply a downsampling operation 20 
times to generate low-resolution inputs, where the scale factor is set 
as r ∈ [1, 4] for ASSR. The in-scale refers to the case when r ∈ [1, 4]; oth-
erwise, it is called the out-scale, which means more challenging settings. 
A patch of size 128 x 128 is randomly extracted from the input image 
for training. To improve data diversity, data augmentation is applied 
with a 50 % probability. The augmentation techniques include left-right 
flipping, up-down flipping, and diagonal inversion.

In addition to the DIV2K validation set, we evaluate our model on 
four widely used benchmark datasets: Set5 [82], Set14 [83], B100 [84], 
and Urban100 [51]. These datasets provide a diverse set of images, 
ensuring a comprehensive evaluation of our model across various im-
age types and complexities. Set5 is a small dataset consisting of five 
high-quality images commonly used as a baseline for super-resolution 
evaluation. It contains well-defined edges and sharp textures, making 
it suitable for assessing fundamental reconstruction quality. Set14 in-
cludes 14 images with diverse content, ranging from natural landscapes 
to artificial objects. The dataset is more challenging than Set5, as it 
contains complex textures and varying structures that require precise 
reconstruction. B100 is derived from the Berkeley Segmentation Dataset 
and consists of 100 natural images. It is particularly challenging due to 
its high texture complexity and natural image diversity, making it a ro-
bust benchmark for real-world super-resolution performance. Urban100 
contains 100 high-resolution images of urban scenes, featuring intricate 
architectural structures and repetitive patterns. This dataset is espe-
cially valuable for evaluating a model’s ability to restore high-frequency 
details and structural consistency in complex urban environments. In 
this paper, we use the DIV2K validation set, Set5, Set14, B100, and 
Urban100 as benchmark datasets for evaluation. These datasets collec-
tively ensure that our model is rigorously tested across various image 
types, scales, and complexities, providing a thorough assessment of its 
super-resolution performance.

The model is trained using the Adam optimizer [85] with a default 
learning rate of 4 x 10 -5 . Additionally, the Sobolev exponent s in Eq. (5) 
is updated with a higher learning rate of 1 x 10 -4 . To stabilize training 
and improve convergence, we adopt the CosineAnnealingLR learning 
rate scheduler [86]. Furthermore, a warm-up strategy is applied for the 
first 50 epochs, where the learning rate starts at 10 times the base value 
and gradually decreases. The batch size for training is set to 64, and the 
total number of training epochs is 1050 (following SRNO [28]).

The proposed model adopts EDSR-baseline [9] as the encoder to ex-
tract initial spatial features from the input image. Following this, the 
network is composed of T = 3 SoFoNO blocks, each with C b = 256 chan-
nels. The initial value of the parameter s, which plays a critical role in 
characterizing the behavior of the Sobolev Branch, is set to 0. This initial-
ization corresponds to the standard L 2 setting, enabling the network to 
adaptively learn the necessary frequency-domain characteristics during 
training (see Fig. 2 and Eq. 5). In addition, the weight α of the Sobolev 
loss function, which balances the contribution of the frequency-domain 
regularization, is set to 1.

In super-resolution (SR), PSNR is the de facto primary metric for 
quantitative evaluation, measuring pixel-wise reconstruction fidelity 
with respect to the GT. We additionally report SSIM [87] and LPIPS [88] 
to assess structural similarity and perceptual quality. Specifically, SSIM 
quantifies how well the structural information is preserved in the recon-
structed image, while LPIPS compares deep feature representations to 
measure perceptual similarity.

Recent SR-specific quality assessors have also been explored along-
side the standard metrics. DeepSRQ [89] introduces a no-reference 
two-stream CNN that separately models structure- and texture-related

degradations characteristic of SR artifacts, using stride-based adap-
tive cropping to balance the training data. Building on this landscape, 
SFSN [90] frames SR quality in a two-dimensional space of structural 
fidelity and statistical naturalness, clarifying the typical trade-off be-
tween fidelity-oriented SISR methods and naturalness-oriented GAN 
approaches, and fusing the two cues through a simple linear combina-
tion. SRIF [91] adopts a complementary view in a deterministic-fidelity 
versus statistical-fidelity plane, describes characteristic clustering of 
existing algorithms along this axis, and integrates the two fidelities 
via content-dependent uncertainty weighting informed by sharpness 
and texture. More recently, BiAtten-Net [92] presents a full-reference 
design that decouples SR generation and evaluation and employs bi-
directional attention to emphasize distortions in both processes, in line 
with human-visual-system considerations.

In this work, we adopt PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS because they are 
widely standardized across common SR benchmarks, enabling fair and 
reproducible comparisons with prior work. These metrics provide com-
plementary perspectives by capturing fidelity via PSNR, structural sim-
ilarity via SSIM, and perceptual realism via LPIPS, with well-tested 
implementations that facilitate reliable replication.

The model is implemented in Python version 3.9 using the PyTorch 
[93] deep learning framework version 2.6.0 and Torchvision version 
0.21.0. We leverage CUDA 12.4 for GPU acceleration to enhance train-
ing efficiency, and rely on cuDNN 9.1.0.70. For image processing and 
numerical operations, we use NumPy 2.0.2, SciPy 1.13.1, and OpenCV 
4.11.0.86. The experiments are conducted on an NVIDIA A100 80 GB 
GPU under this software configuration. In this environment, we require 
approximately 66 h to complete 1050 training iterations.

on the DIV2K validation set compared to state-of-the-art methods, 
including MetaSR [12], LIIF [14], LTE [15], and SRNO [28] and 
GaussianSR [44]. The results clearly indicate that when using EDSR-
baseline as an encoder, SoFoNO outperforms previous methods, reinforc-
ing its effectiveness in high-quality image reconstruction. Furthermore, 
Table 2 highlights that SoFoNO achieves outstanding results not only on 
the DIV2K validation set but also across multiple benchmark datasets, 
including Set5, Set14, B100, and Urban100. These results affirm the gen-
eralization capability of our method across diverse datasets and image 
types.

SISR at extreme scales such as x20 and x30 is a highly challeng-
ing task due to the severe loss of high-frequency details. Conventional 
methods often struggle to reconstruct fine textures at such high magni-
fications, leading to noticeable artifacts and loss of structural integrity. 
Despite these difficulties, pushing the limits of SR is essential for real-
world applications requiring extreme upscaling, such as satellite imaging 
[3] and medical imaging [94]. In this work, we explore these chal-
lenging tasks and demonstrate that SoFoNO can effectively restore fine 
details even at extreme scales. As shown in Fig. 8, SoFoNO consistently 
achieves superior reconstruction quality, particularly evident in the field 
pattern at x20, which remains clear and well-defined. Furthermore, at 
x27, SoFoNO effectively captures the intricate building patterns, outper-
forming conventional methods. These results highlight the robustness 
of SoFoNO in handling extreme-scale SR tasks, further validating its 
effectiveness across various practical applications.

SR techniques are not limited to natural image benchmarks but can 
also be extended to the medical imaging domain, where high-resolution 
information is often crucial for diagnosis and treatment planning. In 
this work, we further validate our method on medical imaging data, 
specifically focusing on brain CT scans with tumor cases.

We employ the CT–Xray Dataset, a publicly available medical imag-
ing dataset obtained from Kaggle, which contains a diverse collection 
of CT and X-ray images with colorized representations designed to en-
hance diagnostic interpretability. For our experiments, we primarily 
used brain CT tumor cases, comprising 840 training and 48 testing 
images with a resolution of 512 x 512, and total dataset sizes of approx-
imately 33 M and 2 M for training and testing, respectively. The dataset 
encompasses images acquired under clinically relevant conditions and 
typical diagnostic settings, ensuring that the data distribution and visual 
characteristics closely reflect real-world medical imaging scenarios.

We applied our approach to the tumor dataset and compared the re-
constructed results against representative baselines. As shown in Fig. 9, 
our method achieves superior quantitative performance, consistently 
producing higher PSNR and SSIM scores, while also yielding lower LPIPS 
values. More importantly, the qualitative results indicate that our recon-
structions preserve fine structural details and enhance tumor boundaries 
more clearly than competing methods.

These findings demonstrate the potential applicability of our SR 
framework to the medical imaging field, suggesting that it can be a 
valuable tool for improving image quality in clinical practice where ac-
quiring high-resolution scans may be infeasible due to hardware, cost, 
or radiation dose constraints.

When s is fixed to a constant value, such as s = 1 or s = 2, the 
model achieves relatively high performance at the beginning of train-
ing, iteration 1. However, by the end of training, iteration 300, these 
fixed settings result in lower performance. In contrast, allowing s to be 
learnable improves overall stability and ensures consistent performance 
gains. A more detailed analysis in Table 5 reveals that under the setting
α = 1, s = 1 s = 2 yield high PSNR and SSIM at iteration 1, but their per
formance deteriorates as training progresses. On the other hand, setting
s as a learnable parameter not only maintains competitive performance 
in the early stages but also achieves superior results in the later itera
tions. These findings suggest that making s learnable is the most effective 
approach, as it provides both initial stability and long-term performance 
improvements across training iterations.

We perform an ablation study to assess the impact of each archi-
tectural component, which is composed of the local branch, the sobolev

branch, and the cross-mixing module, on overall performance. As shown 
in Table 6, although removing the local branch maintains comparable 
PSNR to the full model, it significantly degrades perceptual quality and 
overall consistency. While the removal of the sobolev branch leads to 
slightly better LPIPS at most scales, it consistently underperforms in 
PSNR and fails to match the balanced performance of the full model. 
The exclusion of the cross mixing module results in the largest perfor-
mance degradation, confirming its crucial role in feature integration. 
Our model is architecturally and loss-functionally biased toward precise 
reconstruction and frequency fidelity, which aligns well with PSNR and 
SSIM, but not with the perceptual diversity and realism emphasized by 
LPIPS.

When a neural network is trained, it generally exhibits a tendency to 
learn low-frequency components before moving on to high-frequency 
details, a phenomenon known as spectral bias [95]. This occurs due 
to the architectural properties of the network and the way it is ini-
tialized, resulting in simpler, smoother features (i.e., low-frequency 
information) being learned before more complex, high-frequency pat-
terns. Early in the training process, the model quickly reduces error 
by adapting to low-frequency regions that vary less rapidly. As training

In this paper, we propose SoFoNO for arbitrary-scale super-
resolution, leveraging a specialized transformation method that operates 
in the frequency domain. Specifically, we modulate the amplitude in ac-
cordance with the order s by applying the Bessel potential space, thereby
allowing the model to effectively capture and incorporate subtle varia-
tions in frequency components. In addition, we integrate the derivative
order, extracted during the learning process, into the Sobolev loss by 
utilizing the FFT. This helps stabilize the training dynamics and ensures

Through an extensive series of experiments, we have observed that 
our method demonstrates compelling capabilities in preserving fine de-
tails and edge information while maintaining strong robustness across 
different scaling factors. The results strongly indicate that our approach 
possesses sufficient potential and competitiveness to stand alongside 
other frequency-domain super-resolution techniques. Overall, the syn-
ergy of Bessel potential space, frequency-based amplitude modulation,

and derivative order integration within the Sobolev loss provides a pow-
erful and flexible foundation for future research and applications in 
high-quality image upscaling.
